blocks.text: Opus 5.5 能精准遵循指令、不越出范围，因此它产出的表格、幻灯片和文档往往只需稍作修改。它对数字和来源也很谨慎。在一次内部研究测试中，Opus 5.5 仅凭一份保存下来的网页快照撰写某公司季度业绩报告，而该公司的财报在这份快照里很难找到。自动评分器会对照快照中的页面核查每一个数字和引文，只要有一处数字或引文是编造的，报告即判为不合格。在各个 effort 档位下，它的 18 份报告中有 16 份通过。

blocks.text: 可以先试这些任务

inlines.text: 可以先试这些任务
直接要成品文件。
如果你想要表格或文档，就直接要表格或文档，而不是要一份提纲再自己搭建。多数情况下，Opus 5.5 能一次就从你的需求做到成品文件。
让它检查长文档。
给它一份长计划、报告或演示文稿，让它找出错误和不一致之处。Opus 5.5 能发现长文档中容易漏掉的细节，比如演示文稿里的某张图表与其源数据对不上。
交给它一个研究问题。
提一个没有既定答案的问题，让它汇总各方资料、通读长文档，再把发现写成备忘录、报告或演示文稿。
试试视觉类工作。
它在视觉能力上的提升同样适用于设计，可以试着用它做界面原型、搭建网站，或者为某个概念配图。

blocks.alt: illustration of tasks for claude opus 5.5

blocks.text: 改掉这几个提示词习惯

inlines.text: 改掉这几个提示词习惯
把 Claude 接入你的工作文件和系统。
这是让输出贴合你实际工作的最有用步骤之一：通过连接器让 Claude 访问你的文件和系统后，它就能自己去取任务所需的内容，而不只是依赖你粘贴进来的部分。在 Team 和 Enterprise 套餐中，需要由所有者先开启连接器，成员才能使用。
在第一条消息里说清楚“完成”是什么样。
不要一条条地下指令，而是直接描述你的目标、最终产出，以及你希望它在什么时候停下来问你。相比 Opus 5，Opus 5.5 更能把冗长、多环节的工作一路推进到底。
删掉“仔细想”“认真思考”这类话。
Opus 5.5 的思考功能始终开启，它会根据你的请求和努力程度自行决定思考多少。在我们的测试中，删掉这些句子后回复开始得更快，质量也没有明显下降。
从 Medium 努力程度开始。
Medium 是 Opus 5.5 的默认档位，在我们的编程和知识工作评测中，Medium 档的 Opus 5.5 与 High 档的 Opus 5 持平甚至更好。更高的档位思考更久、花费更多，但未必产出更好的结果，所以等 Medium 卡住了再升到 High。要更改设置，点击发送按钮旁的模型名称，选择 Effort。
直接附上图表，而不是重新录入。
把图表、截图或示意图本身发过去，而不是把其中的数字抄进提示词。为早期模型设计的变通做法，比如把图表数值转写出来，现在可能已经不需要了。
点名你不想要的风格。
做设计时，像“避免千篇一律”这样的笼统指令，往往只是把一种默认风格换成另一种。具体点出要避开的样式效果更好，比如米色背景或胶囊形按钮。
把你的品牌风格交给它。
把品牌或写作规范粘贴到请求里，或者让 Claude 参考你现有的优秀演示文稿——比如它能通过连接器访问的 Google Drive 文件夹——并要求它照着做。要做好几轮才能完全对味。

blocks.text: Claude 发现，数据并不支持这四种理论中的任何一种，不过其中有一种无法完全排除。随后它提出了一个此前没人提过的解释：新店开得离老店太近，把老店的销售额抢走了。按城市排列门店时，这个规律不太明显；一旦按与新店的距离筛选，规律就清晰了。Claude 又用销售额影响对这段距离做回归，为这一发现提供了佐证。

blocks.text: Opus 5.5 follows instructions precisely and stays in scope, so the spreadsheets, slides, and documents it produces often need little editing. It's careful with figures and sources, too. In one internal research test, Opus 5.5 wrote reports on a company's quarterly performance using only a saved snapshot of the web, in which the company’s earnings release was hard to locate. An automated grader checked every figure and quote against the pages in that snapshot, under a condition that the report would fail if even a single figure or quote was invented. Across effort settings, 16 of its 18 reports passed.

blocks.text: Try these tasks first

inlines.text: Try these tasks first
Ask for a finished file.

If you want a spreadsheet or a document, ask for the spreadsheet or document rather than an outline to build from. More often than not, Opus 5.5 can get from your request to the finished file in one pass.
Have it check long documents.

Give it a long plan, report, or deck and ask it to find mistakes and inconsistencies. Opus 5.5 catches details that are easy to miss in long documents, such as a chart in a deck that doesn’t match its source data.
Hand it a research question.
Ask a question without a set answer and have it pull sources together, work through long documents, and write up what it finds as a memo, report, or deck.
Try visual work.
Its vision gains carry over to design, so try it for prototyping an interface, building a website, or illustrating a concept.

blocks.text: Change these prompting habits

inlines.text: Change these prompting habits
Connect Claude to your work files and systems.

This is one of the most useful steps for getting output that fits your work, because when Claude can reach your files and systems through connectors, it can go get what a task needs instead of working only from what you paste in. On Team and Enterprise plans, an owner has to turn a connector on before members can use it.
Say what done looks like in your first message.

Instead of prompting Claude with instructions one at a time, describe your goal, the finished output, and when you want it to stop and ask. Opus 5.5 carries long, multipart work through to the end better than Opus 5 did.
Delete “think hard” and “think carefully.”

Thinking is always on for Opus 5.5, and it decides how much to think based on your request and the effort level. In our testing, removing those lines made replies start sooner, with no clear drop in quality.
Start at Medium effort.

Medium is the default for Opus 5.5, and on our coding and knowledge-work evaluations, Opus 5.5 at Medium matched or beat Opus 5 at High. Higher settings think longer and cost more without always producing better work, so move up to High when Medium stalls. To change the setting, click the model name next to the send button and choose Effort.
Attach the chart instead of retyping it.
Share the chart, screenshot, or diagram itself rather than copying its numbers into the prompt. Workarounds built for earlier models, like transcribing a chart's values, may no longer be needed.
Name the styles you don't want.

For design work, a general instruction like “avoid a generic look” tends to swap one default style for another. Naming specific patterns to avoid, such as a cream background or pill-shaped buttons, works better.
Give it your house style.

Paste your brand or writing guidelines into the request, or point Claude to your best existing decks, for example in a Google Drive folder it can reach through a connector, and ask it to match them. Expect a few rounds before it's exactly right.

blocks.text: Here's what all this looks like on one project we worked through in a demo. At a hypothetical retail company, revenue growth had slowed over the past year, leadership had four theories about why, and an analyst had a folder of material: spreadsheets of sales by store, PDFs from the latest leadership off-site, and other files. With Opus 5.5 at Medium effort, the prompt read, roughly:

inlines.text: Here's what all this looks like on one project we worked through in a demo. At a hypothetical retail company, revenue growth had slowed over the past year, leadership had four theories about why, and an analyst had a folder of material: spreadsheets of sales by store, PDFs from the latest leadership off-site, and other files. With Opus 5.5 at Medium effort, the prompt read, roughly:

blocks.text: Growth slowed a lot this year. Leadership has a couple of theories about why; they're in [my manager's] note. Everything I have is in the uploaded folder. Please test each of the four theories against the data and tell me which ones hold up.

inlines.text: Growth slowed a lot this year. Leadership has a couple of theories about why; they're in [my manager's] note. Everything I have is in the uploaded folder. Please test each of the four theories against the data and tell me which ones hold up.

blocks.text: The prompt doesn't tell Claude to think hard, and it doesn't say which file to check for which theory. It states the goal and what the final output looks like, and leaves the approach to Claude.

inlines.text: The prompt doesn't tell Claude to think hard, and it doesn't say which file to check for which theory. It states the goal and what the final output looks like, and leaves the approach to Claude.

blocks.text: Claude found that the data didn't support any of the four theories, though one couldn't be fully ruled out. It then proposed an explanation that nobody had raised: new stores had opened too close to existing ones and were drawing sales away from them. The pattern was a little unclear with the stores listed by city, and clear once they were filtered by proximity to a new store. Claude backed the finding with a regression of the sales impact against that distance.
